newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No Balts in NATO, Yeltsin tells Finnish leader.
newsitem.headline: No Balts in NATO, Yeltsin tells Finnish leader.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin spoke out angrily on Sunday against any NATO move to absorb the former Soviet Baltic states.
Slipping into a more relaxed vein, however, he then boasted of his prowess in beating Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari with bundled twigs in a traditional Russian steam bath, or 'banya'.
"We went fishing, rode on a boat, we were in the banya,' Yeltsin told reporters after a crisp, sunny day with Ahtisaari at his lakeside holiday retreat in the northern Karelia region.
'And the Russian president really knows how to whip the twigs," Yeltsin added. The practice, indispensible to the serious Russian banya go-er, is reputed to stimulate blood circulation.

Yeltsin, continuing his apparently strong recovery from heart bypass surgery last November, showed no lack of vigour in warning against any NATO move to draw Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia into its ranks.

"I expressed, of course, our dissatisfaction with the Madrid Communique as it mentions the Baltics as new (potential) states and that's dangerous," Yeltsin told reporters after a second day of talks with Ahtisaari.
He referred to a NATO summit in Madrid last week during which it invited three ex-Soviet allies -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- to join.
Yeltsin was an early advocate of independence for the Baltic states when he was locked in a power struggle with Mikhail Gorbachev in the last months of the Soviet Union.
But their loss poses security questions for the new Russia he leads, robbing it of forward air defences and naval bases.
Admitting them, NATO would reach Russia's borders for the first time, and surround the isolated Kaliningrad region, annexed from Germany after 1945, by two new members -- Poland and Lithuania.
Finland is neutral but pledges to work closely with NATO. It has no immediate plans to try to join.

After a meeting in St Petersburg on Sunday with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said NATO reserved the option of inviting the Baltic states into the alliance.

"We have said all along that NATO is open to all democratic market systems in Europe...It doesn't matter where a country is on the map, they are eligible for membership in NATO," she told Russian television.
Ahtisaari appeared cool to the Russian president's suggestion on Saturday that Moscow and Helsinki mount joint border patrols.
But the Finnish president did say there was room for improvement in the way the two frontier services work together on their 1270-km (790-mile) border.
